summary: Minnesota Point Light marked Superior Entry from 1858 to 1885; only the lower half of its brick tower remains on the Duluth sandbar.

access.note: LighthouseFriends: grounds open, tower closed; the U.S. Lighthouse Society record says not open to the public. Owned by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (LighthouseFriends). Driving past Sky Harbor Airport is not permitted; walk about 1.5 miles.

corrections.why: The tower light went dark for good on 6 August 1885 (LighthouseFriends; Pepper; USLHS disposition 'Discontinued 1885'). The record's 1913 is a Wikidata date with no source read here; the roster's last keeper is 1913.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's conflict list gives 1885 (Rowlett) and 1913 (Wikidata). The sources read here agree on 1885 for the tower light going dark for good. 1878 (USLHS 'Year Discontinued') marks the start of the pierhead light's replacement of the tower light; the tower light came back in 1880 and went out for good in 1885.
The lens order differs: fourth order in LighthouseFriends and the USLHS record, fifth order in Pepper. The facts keep fourth order and the story gives both.

notes_for_editor: Thin primary base: no NRHP nomination (npgallery 74002206 returns the 'not yet digitized' placeholder), and the corpus holds Lighthouse Board reports only for 1891-1901, so nothing from the 1850s to 1880s was read from a Board report. Every 1850s-1880s fact rests on LighthouseFriends and Terry Pepper, and both say they draw on the Board's reports, which were not read. Check the Board reports for 1855-1886 before publication, especially the appropriation date (1854 or 1855) and the lens order (fourth or fifth). Light dates: the record's 1913 deactivation (Wikidata) has no support in the sources read; the USLHS record gives 1878 'discontinued', which was the replacement by the pierhead light, not the final darkening. Keepers after 1885: the roster names keepers under this station until 1913, but LighthouseFriends and Pepper say the keepers left the point in 1894 or 1895. Neither says which light the later keepers tended. The story does not attribute them to the tower. Keeper names match the LighthouseFriends keeper list. Annie Doody: listed twice (1906, 1907) as acting assistant. The archive does not give her relation to Thomas Doody, and this file does not infer one. Position: the record's point (46.710038, -92.025862) agrees with Pepper's GPS (46 deg 42 min 36 s N, 92 deg 1 min 33 s W). The USLHS place record gives 47.2 N and latitude '46 deg 72.00 min' (an impossible minute value). The record us-mn-minnesota-point-2 holds the USLHS point at 47.2, -92.04317 with events 1856 lens, 1857 first lit, 1858 built, 1878 deactivated, and is a duplicate. The editor should merge or drop it. Tower height: the record gives 15.0 m; LighthouseFriends gives a 40-foot (12.2 m) original tower and says only the truncated remains stand. The 15 m figure is not checked here and may describe the current remains. The date when the upper tower was removed is not in any source read. Access conflict: LighthouseFriends says the grounds are open and the tower closed; the USLHS record says the site is not open to the public. Confirm with the Army Corps before publication. The USCG Historian's archived page for Minnesota Point returned only the Wayback Machine frame and was not used. Wrecks: no wreck or rescue tied to the light was found in the sources read; the Life-Saving Service had a station named Minnesota Point on the lists of 1892-1895, which is a separate record and is not discussed here. Confidence is low: every fact rests on secondary histories (LighthouseFriends, Pepper) and the USLHS record; the Board reports they cite were not read, and the appropriation date, lens order and keeper departure conflict. Fact-check 2026-10-27: the 1868 Board quotation is Terry Pepper's, so the story attributes it to Pepper; 'Repairs began early' (not in any source) was removed; the depot appropriation is 1903 (LighthouseFriends), not 1902; only one woman, Annie Doody, is on the USLHS roster (acting-assistant heading, 1906 and 1907). Open for the owner: the story has five chapter headings where the guide's moderate shape allows two to four (about 850 words); it was left as written.
